COVID: Delta Variant

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at how the Delta Variant is driving the 3rd deadly wave of COVID-19

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche investigates the Delta Variant and how it's driving the 3rd deadly wave of COVID-19 by speaking with Dr Tulio De Oliveira, the researcher who has tracked how it's become the dominant strain South Africa.

We also look at how the health system is coping under the strain of the 3rd wave by speaking with doctors & first responders in the front line

Summary:
This past Saturday, South Africa recorded the highest number of new COVID-19 infections since the pandemic began. This illustrates the devastating size of the 3rd COVID-19 wave surging over South Africa currently. Larger in size and scale than ever before, the wave is being driven by the so-called Delta variant that first appeared in India. 30-60% more contagious than previous variants, it is wreaking havoc around the world, having already been detected in 98 countries.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has urged leaders to push back against daunting new COVID surges through increased vaccination efforts and public health measures, warning that with Delta quickly becoming the dominant strain in many countries ‘we are in a very dangerous period of the pandemic’.

Further information:
In this story we explain what the delta variant is and how it differs from previous strains of virus.

We see how it has become the dominant strain of COVID-19 in South Africa by speaking to KRISP director Dr Tulio De Oliviera who has tracked it's progress

We also see the impact of the 3rd wave on the health system by speaking with spokespeople from both public hospitals in Gauteng, as well as private hospitals

We also get a first-person account of what it's like to be on the frontlines of the deadly surge by speaking with Doctors and First Responders working around the clock to save lives

Expert:
Prof. Tulio De Oliveira
Dr. Richard Friedland
Dr. Ntsakisi Maluleke

Press Release:


COVID-19: The Delta Blow
Why did the third wave of the COVID-19 pandemic hit with such ferocity, chasing up infection numbers and flooding hospitals? Carte Blanche analyses the observations of clinicians and scientists on the frontlines dealing with the effects of the highly contagious Delta variant. With hospitals full to capacity as the third wave peaks, will the health system buckle under the strain?
Producer: Julian Sun | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


DELTA VARIANT FINAL SCRIPT FOR VO

Oliver Marshall is an experienced first responder – but he’s never seen anything like this third wave of the pandemic.

OLIVER MARSHALL: As a health care system and industry, we thought that the first and second wave would really prepare us quite well for the third one. But I think we were caught completely off-guard by this mutation in the Delta variant.

60 per cent more transmissible than the original wild-type strain and the Beta variant that caused the second wave, Delta has driven infections during the third wave that peaked at over 208,000 active cases.

MASA LINK: A third wave of covid-19 that was predicted to be milder has now become a worst-case scenario, pushing the health care system in South Africa to the brink of collapse.

PROF. FRANCOIS VENTER: It's severe. Every single indication we have, which is the new infection rates, hospitalisation rates and the death rates, suggest that this wave is far worse than the first two waves.

At Wits University, Professor Francois Venter is a leading communicable diseases specialist.

PROF. FRANCOIS VENTER: The waves in the different provinces have varied from one to the next between the first and second. So, for instance, in the Western Cape, the second wave was worse than the first. The Gauteng third wave is two or three-fold, possibly more-fold.

Delta first appeared in India in December and has been found in 98 countries around the world. It was first detected in South Africa by Professor Tulio de Oliveira, Director of the KwaZulu-Natal Research Innovation and Sequencing Platform, or KRISP, that supports genomics research in Africa.

MASA: The first case of a Delta variant, we reported in South Africa in May. Are you surprised at how quickly it spread across the country?

PROF. TULIO DE OLIVEIRA, DIRECTOR: KZN RESEARCH INNOVATION & SEQUENCING PLATFORM (KRISP): Yes, this was first case were reported in travellers and also in shipping crew. South Africa have some of the biggest harbours in Africa. But in general, it was very surprising to see how quick that has spread and how quick it set up in the population. It was even quicker than the Beta variant.

MASA: How do you go about identifying and tracking this virus the way you've been?

PROF. TULIO DE OLIVEIRA: So the process of identifying, tracking the virus, it is started at accessing remaining samples, so this means samples that has been used for diagnostic in very large laboratories...so we are talking about both private but also the National Health Laboratory Services. And what we do is try to get a very spread geographically sampling, random sampling, that is repeated every week. Once you get the sampling done at the central laboratories, they will move to one of at the moment at eight different genomics facilities in South Africa. And then what we do is to transform these samples into a genome, sequence the genome of the virus.

When the Delta variant emerged in India it caused consternation in the health system.

MASA: We saw what the Delta variant has done in India. You have been recently quoted in the media saying that Gauteng could see themselves where India was.

PROF. FRANCOIS VENTER: And I think some of the other provinces are going to see them where India is, as well as Gauteng,

TULIO DE OLIVEIRA: We see many different variants or lineages co-circulating and the most transmissible one tend to dominate all the infections in a short period of time.

The third wave started in Gauteng, peaking at over ninety-one thousand cases. MediClinic’s Dr. Gerrit de Villiers has an overview of the private sector.

DR GERRIT DE VILLIERS, CHIEF CLINICAL OFFICER: MEDICLINIC: The hospitals are under severe strain and it has been going on for quite a few weeks in many of the regions.

MASA: And when you compare this third wave with the previous to what are some of those differences that you're noting?

DR GERRIT DE VILLIERS: It certainly seems to be a younger population that's ending up in our facilities at the moment. And one of the reasons for that could be that they were not infected with one or two. They have a more social lifestyle. They go out more they are more exposed. And then, of course, we have managed to vaccinate a percentage of our older population in the country already. And even after a few weeks of the first dose of the PFIZER vaccine...there will already be protection for them.

MASA: do you expect it to get worse?

DR GERRIT DE VILLIERS: So our Gauteng facilities are basically at capacity. we expect the same pressure to spread to the rest of the country. I know no one knows how the Delta variant will affect those provinces that at the high incidence in the Second wave, specifically KZN, Eastern Cape and parts of the Garden Route, and we are holding our breath that it will not be as bad as the second wave because that was really very tough for the hospitals to cope with that workload.

Doctors and nurses are taking strain. South African Medical Association Chairperson Dr Angelique Coetzee says some of her members struggle more to treat patients infected by Delta.

DR ANGELIQUE COETZEE, CHAIR: SOUTH AFRICAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION: So what we have seen is a lot of general practitioners, are not seeing the patients covered patients...they make the diagnosis on a lab result and then they will give them a standardised prescription. And and COVID-19 is not a standardized disease. You have to examine your patient. If you want to do it via zoom, then you need to make sure the patient's got a oximeter at the home which you can access to see with what is this saturation levels of the patient's oxygen. You need to make sure the pulse is right. You need to make sure the patient's got a blood pressure monitor and you need to make sure that there is a way that you can look into the throat of the patient.

Keeping caregivers safe means relying on remote patient monitoring devices.

DR ANGELIQUE COETZEE: if the patient have that, then you can see the patient over zoom...we are asking from SAMA-side, our general practitioners, please examine your patients. Please put your hand on them. And if you are afraid, contact us. We will tell you how to make sure that your surgery are safe. I only have lost two patients...And we are using what I have been trying to do...common sense, good principles, good clinical skills and looking after your patient.

Hospitals full to capacity exacerbates the strain on first responders.

OLIVER MARSHALL, GENERAL MANAGER: MEDI RESPONSE: You'll see we've got a live dashboard in which we track every health care facility in the Johannesburg area and we know where which hospital is available and what capacity they are at and during the call, our controllers are constantly following up with hospitals to say, can you accept this…

OMPHILE MOATSHE, BASIC LIFE SUPPORT MEDIC: we wait like outside for a long time and then from the hospital, we have to come back to the base. We have to make sure that we thoroughly decontaminate the ambulance. And then one day we go to another call. So you just call after call. Having to see families in pain, you know, having to see people dying, It's it's a lot to take in. So I'm taking I'm emotionally exhausted. I am physically exhausted. But we have to keep on going. This is what we signed up for.

As the wave in Gauteng looks set to be mirrored in other provinces, vaccines provide the only way out. At the National Institute for Communicable Diseases Professor Penny Moore has crunched the numbers.

PROF. PENNY MOORE, NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR COMMUNICABLE DISEASES: I think at the very beginning of this pandemic, we all hoped that we were dealing with a single variant and it was and spread across the world. But our vaccines, which we had shown, worked very well against that variant would be fine. And then Beta emerged beta, the second wave variant in our country was incredibly resistant to all antibodies. It's I think one of the most resistant variants has been described perhaps on par with the Gamma from Brazil. And but that really worried us in terms of how well our vaccines would deal with it. We have laboratory data now for AstraZeneca and for Pfizer and Johnson and Johnson, all three vaccines we show that those vaccines are much better able to deal with Delta and they would have been able to deal with Beta. So although we have Delta now throughout our country and and a huge problem with transmissibility, which is driving the huge numbers of infections. On the flip side, the one ray of hope is that actually Delta is much less resistant than beta.

PROF. FRANCOIS VENTER: I think we're fairly confident there's going to be a fourth wave in November and December. For that, we have to accelerate the vaccine vaccination program. Otherwise we're going to be having the same conversation in six months time.


PROMOS:

IN-STUDIO: Why did COVID-19’s third wave hit with such ferocity…spiking infection numbers…flooding hospitals? Medics on the frontline unpack the impact of the most transmissible Delta variant.

TONIGHT: With hospitals full to capacity as the third wave of COVID-19 infection peaks – we investigate how the health system is holding up under the strain of the highly infectious Delta variant.

SOCIAL: Once predicted to be milder, the third wave of COVID-19 has become a worst-case scenario, due to the highly transmissible Delta variant. Scientists analyse Delta’s impacted on patient care.
